Bone & Soft Tissue Tumour Pathology: Must-Know Diagnoses — CAT: MCQs

faq.a: Yes, in a febrile patient with severe features and high malaria prevalence, start IV artesunate empirically while awaiting test results.
faq.q: Can I start antimalarials before confirming malaria?

faq.a: Artesunate reduces mortality and has fewer cardiac and hypoglycaemic side‑effects than quinine.
faq.q: Why avoid quinine if artesunate is available?

faq.a: Give rapid crystalloid bolus (20 mL/kg), start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and monitor clinical response.
faq.q: What is the first step if a patient is in septic shock and labs are unavailable?

exam: A 4‑year‑old with fever, pallor and a positive malaria test presents with a GCS of 7 – what immediate actions are required? — Secure airway, give IV artesunate, start fluid resuscitation, and arrange urgent transfer for possible intensive care.

A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive man has cough, weight loss and haemoptysis; sputum is unavailable – how do you differentiate TB from severe malaria? — Look for malaria exposure, perform rapid test; if negative, treat as presumptive TB and start anti‑TB therapy while arranging imaging.

Why is IV ceftriaxone preferred over oral amoxicillin for community‑acquired sepsis in this setting? — Provides reliable high serum levels, covers common gram‑negative organisms, and avoids absorption issues in sick patients.

A patient with sickle‑cell disease develops chest pain and new infiltrates on X‑ray – what diagnosis should you consider and how to manage? — Acute chest syndrome; give oxygen, IV antibiotics, blood transfusion if indicated, and avoid fluid overload.
What red‑flag sign on examination would make you suspect impending respiratory failure in severe malaria? — Inability to speak full sentences, respiratory rate >30/min, and use of accessory muscles.

How would you adjust management if the laboratory cannot measure serum bilirubin in a jaundiced patient? — Use clinical signs (yellow sclera, dark urine) and assess for encephalopathy; start supportive care and avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
Explain why a patient with fulminant hepatitis should not receive acetaminophen even for fever. — The liver is already injured; acetaminophen can cause further hepatic necrosis and worsen outcomes.

When is it appropriate to give a blood transfusion in severe malaria, and why is the threshold higher than in other anaemias? — Transfuse when Hb <7 g/dL or there is lactic acidosis, because malaria causes microvascular obstruction and rapid tissue hypoxia.
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A concise guide to the most frequently encountered life‑threatening conditions in East African hospitals, focusing on clinical reasoning, limited investigations and urgent management.

b: Life‑threatening if untreated
Require immediate decision‑making
Often present with overlapping signs
sections.p: Critical diagnoses are conditions that, if missed or delayed, cause rapid deterioration or death. They are identified by a combination of history, bedside examination and essential tests.

b: Mild – stable vitals, no organ failure
Moderate – one organ dysfunction, still conscious
Severe – multiple organ failure, hypotension, altered mental state
sections.p: Severity is judged by organ dysfunction (e.g., shock, altered consciousness) rather than disease‑specific scores, which may be unavailable.

b: Severe malaria (Plasmodium falciparum)
Acute bacterial sepsis (e.g., typhoid, pneumonia)
Pulmonary TB with massive haemoptysis
Sickle‑cell crisis with acute chest syndrome
Rheumatic heart disease decompensation
Hepatitis B fulminant liver failure
Herbal or drug‑induced nephrotoxicity
sections.p: In low‑resource East Africa the common precipitants are infections, haemoglobinopathies and toxic exposures.

b: Fever, chills, malaise
Dyspnoea, cough, chest pain
Jaundice, dark urine, right‑upper‑quadrant pain
Severe abdominal pain, vomiting
Altered mental status or seizures
sections.p: Patients often arrive with non‑specific systemic features plus organ‑specific clues.
Use the most informative test that is locally available; if unavailable, rely on clinical surrogates.

t.b: Confirms Plasmodium infection; a positive result directs antimalarial therapy
Detects anaemia, leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia; guides infection vs haemolysis
Identifies hypoglycaemia as a reversible cause of altered consciousness
Assesses renal function; rising creatinine signals acute kidney injury
Looks for infiltrates, pleural effusion or cardiomegaly; if unavailable, use lung auscultation findings
Detects protein, blood or bilirubin; helps differentiate renal vs hepatic causes

b: Systolic BP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg
Respiratory rate >30/min or <8/min
GCS ≤ 8
Unexplained massive haematemesis or haemoptysis
Rapidly falling haemoglobin (>2 g/dL in 24 h)
sections.p: Recognise signs that herald imminent collapse.

b: Airway, breathing, circulation – give oxygen, IV fluids (crystalloids 20 mL/kg) and treat shock promptly
Severe malaria – IV artesunate (preferred) or quinine if artesunate unavailable; avoid monotherapy with chloroquine
Sepsis – broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) within 1 h; de‑escalate when cultures return
Acute chest syndrome – oxygen, antibiotics, blood transfusion if Hb <7 g/dL, avoid fluid overload
Fulminant hepatitis – supportive care, avoid hepatotoxic drugs, consider N‑acetylcysteine if acetaminophen related
Renal failure – avoid nephrotoxic drugs, consider dialysis if available
sections.p: Stabilise first, then treat the underlying cause with drugs that are safe, affordable and available.

b: Repeat vitals and labs every 6 h until stable
Educate on insecticide‑treated nets, prompt malaria treatment, vaccination, safe herbal use
Screen for sickle‑cell disease and provide prophylactic penicillin where indicated
Link to chronic disease clinics for TB, HIV, rheumatic fever
sections.p: Arrange early review and address modifiable risk factors.

b: Severe malaria vs bacterial sepsis – malaria test distinguishes; both may need antibiotics if co‑infection suspected
Acute viral hepatitis vs drug‑induced liver injury – history of drug exposure and acetaminophen level help differentiate
Pulmonary embolism vs TB haemoptysis – ECG and D‑dimer not reliable; chest X‑ray and clinical context guide
sections.p: Conditions that share systemic signs but need different treatment.

b: Rapid malaria test may miss low‑parasitaemia; consider thick smear if suspicion high
Creatinine may be normal early in acute kidney injury; monitor urine output
Chest X‑ray can appear normal in early pulmonary oedema; rely on auscultation
sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or misleading findings in low‑resource labs.

whenToSeekHelp: Unresponsive patient, severe hypotension, uncontrolled bleeding, sudden respiratory failure, or any rapid deterioration despite initial measures
